html:
The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World are a list of seven famous buildings and statues of the ancient Mediterranean and Near East, drawn up by Greek writers after Alexander's conquests opened the eastern world to Greek travellers. The best known version comes from the poet Antipater of Sidon in the 2nd century BCE.

The classic list:

  • the Great Pyramid of Giza, the oldest and the only one still standing;
  • the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, which may never have existed as described;
  • the statue of Zeus by Phidias in the Temple of Zeus at Olympia;
  • the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus;
  • the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, the tomb of the Carian ruler Mausolus, which gave us the word mausoleum;
  • the Colossus of Rhodes, a bronze statue of the sun god;
  • the Lighthouse of Alexandria.

Some early lists put the walls of Babylon in place of the lighthouse. Most of the wonders fell to earthquakes, fire or looting; the Colossus stood for only about half a century. The list as we know it was fixed in the Renaissance.
